page: Microsoft Azure M64ls is a dedicated virtual machine instance belonging to the MS family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. It features 64 vCPUs mapped to 32 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 8280M processor with an x86_64 architecture. The processor operates at a base clock speed of 2.7 GHz and includes 32 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 38 MB L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 512.0 GB of system memory, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. It includes 2097 GB of local storage and is premium storage capable, but does not feature any GPUs or complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark data reveals a significant performance disparity between single-core and multi-core operations. Single-core performance is consistently weak, with stress-ng single-core CPU, Geekbench single-core, gzip compression, and bzip3 decompression all falling into the bottom 10% of tested servers. Conversely, multi-core execution scales to average levels, as demonstrated by stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and bzip3 multi-threaded decompression scoring in the middle 50%. Memory performance is a notable strength, with large-block read-only memory bandwidth reaching 210.73 GB/sec, placing it in the top 25% of servers, while write bandwidth and small-block read bandwidth remain in the average tier.

The instance is suited for memory-intensive workloads that can leverage parallel processing rather than single-threaded speed. Database operations and Redis SET operations perform at average levels, registering 40.62 million operations per second. Static web serving throughput is also average at 29.01 GB/sec. Large language model inference is highly constrained; while prompt processing for small and medium models achieves average speeds, text generation falls into the bottom 10% due to single-core limitations. Given the dedicated hardware allocation and substantial memory capacity, this instance offers a specialized resource profile where the cost efficiency is optimized for parallelized database tasks and memory-bound applications rather than compute-heavy or single-threaded workloads.
